title: Fallback taxonomy and safe upgrade orchestration for Dedicated/Private control planes
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement: Our Dedicated and Private control planes must tolerate partial failures, region partitions, and rolling upgrades without causing broad tenant outages or SLO regressions. Current ad-hoc fallback behavior mixes circuit-breaker thresholds, device-level throttles, and manual runbook steps; this leads to inconsistent tenant isolation during incidents and risky upgrade windows for customers on Private deployments.

Goal: Define a clear taxonomy of fallback strategies (graceful-routing, fractional-shed, tenant-score isolation, model-variant fallback) and implement an orchestrator that enforces them during capacity pressure and rolling upgrades. The orchestrator should be policy-driven, observable, reversible, and compatible with VPC/private control planes.

Scope: Dedicated (reserved pools) and Private (customer-managed control planes) control planes. Excludes Hosted multi-tenant public pools. Workstreams include: policy design, orchestrator implementation, canary upgrade flow, preflight validation, observability integration, and runbook automation.

Design summary and decisions:
- Fallback taxonomy: define three orthogonal axes: (1) routing fallback (route to cheaper/compatible model variant or region), (2) shedding policy (fractional token or request-level shedding by route tags), (3) tenant isolation (score and soft-quarantine with progressive limits). Each axis can be composed to form safe fallback profiles (e.g., "conservative-upgrade", "aggressive-shed").
- Circuit-breaker thresholds: use per-tenant and per-route sliding-window error and latency budgets tied to SLOs (p50/p95 response latency and success-rate). Default thresholds map to P99 latency and 99.9% success for enterprise tiers; for Dedicated we expose configurable headroom.
- Multi-region failover: adopt active-passive for Private by default (respecting local data locality constraints) with optional active-active for tenants who opt in. Failover orchestration will prefer intra-region warm-warm failover, then cross-region with controlled ramping and traffic shaping.
- Upgrade safety: implement staged canary waves at tenant-shard granularity with preflight synthetic traffic (smoke/eval prompts) and KV-cache warmup validation. Canary wave succeeds iff no SLO regressions and specific resource amplification metrics (memory/KV miss rate) remain within thresholds.
- Admission controller integration: admission controller will integrate with orchestrator to enforce per-tenant concurrency and admission budgets when load-shedding is active. This prevents noisy neighbors from consuming resources during upgrades or incidents.
- Reversibility: orchestrator must support automated rollback triggers (SLO breach or abnormal resource metrics) and a controlled backoff window to mitigate thrash.

Trade-offs considered:
- Conservative fallbacks keep availability but increase cost (more cross-region traffic / spin-up). Aggressive shedding reduces cost and maintains latency for top customers but increases error rates for lower-tier tenants. We default to conservative for E tier and more aggressive for trial tiers.
- Active-active gives lower failover latency but complicates consistency and billing; thus opt-in only.

Implementation plan (high-level):
1) Policy DSL and taxonomy (2 wks): author a JSON/YAML policy schema for fallback profiles and thresholds.
2) Orchestrator core (3 wks): state machine that evaluates telemetry (SLOs, admission, KV hit rates) and issues actions (route-update, shed-command, tenant-quarantine).
3) Admission controller hooks (2 wks): ensure per-tenant enforced budgets and graceful rejection messages with retry guidance.
4) Canary/upgrade flow (2 wks): integrate with deployment pipeline to run waves, synthetic checks, and automatic rollback.
5) Observability & runbooks (1 wk): dashboards, alerts, and automated runbook links surfaced in Console.
6) Private deployment compatibility (ongoing): document networking assumptions, provide a fall-back-only operator mode for air-gapped installs.

Testing and validation:
- Chaos tests: region partition, sudden 5x tenant spike, and rolling upgrade with intentional KV-warmup delay.
- Canary scoring: baseline 5 eval prompts and latency percentiles; require <5% relative latency regression for canary pass.
- Tenant-level e2e: synthetic tenants with mixed workloads to validate isolation and admission behavior.

Runbooks and artifacts:
- Confluence: https://confluence.internal.redwood/reliability/fallback-taxonomy (draft)
- GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/1234 (core state machine)
- Dashboard mock: https://grafana.redwood/s/dedicated-fallbacks (private)

Acceptance criteria (done when):
- Policy DSL committed and documented in repo.
- Orchestrator can execute at least three fallback profiles in staging and revert automatically on SLO breach.
- Rolling upgrade flow integrated with CI that runs synthetic validation and gates traffic shift.
- Console surfaces per-tenant fallback state and an incident playbook link.

Open risks:
- Private/air-gapped control planes may have limited telemetry, reducing orchestrator effectiveness; mitigation: provide a "local-only" mode where operators run preflight and staged manual approval steps.
- Complexity of composition could cause operator confusion; mitigation: include safe default profiles and a policy linter.

Next steps:
- Finalize DSL and sketch the orchestrator API (owner: Marco).
- Prototype orchestrator in staging and run chaos experiments (owner: Aisha).
- Schedule design review with security and applied-ml (action: @security-team, @applied-ml).
comments: 2025-02-18 - Marco Reyes: Initial design doc uploaded; started DSL sketch. Need review on the 'fractional-shed' semantics—does it operate at token or request boundary?
2025-02-20 - Aisha Patel: Decided to implement fractional shedding at request granularity with request-level token accounting to simplify billing reconciliation. Added note to policy DSL.
2025-02-24 - Priya Kapoor (SRE): Reviewed failover plan, requested explicit circuit-breaker cooldown windows and a maximum of 3 auto-rollbacks per hour to avoid thrash. Added to acceptance criteria.

2025-02-27 - Marco Reyes: Pushed prototype state machine to staging (PR 1234). Observed race condition when tenant quota recalculation coincides with canary traffic ramp; investigating locking strategy.
